title: Chirurgie des surfaces conformes : notes manuscrites (s.d., 1983-1984), lettres (1984).

deep.reconstruction:
This page continues a survey of canonical metrics on conformal (Riemann) surfaces, possibly non-orientable and possibly with boundary, organized by the type of the universal cover. It belongs to Grothendieck's 'chirurgie des surfaces conformes' project. The previous page set up the hyperbolic case: X is hyperbolic when its universal cover is the upper half-plane H, equivalently when every conformal map C → X is constant.

(1) End of the hyperbolic case. The Poincaré metric of H has curvature −1 and is invariant under Aut(H) = PSL_2(R), and under the antiholomorphic isometries in the non-orientable case. It therefore descends to a canonical metric on X. When X is compact, this is the unique Riemannian metric compatible with the conformal structure that has constant curvature −1. Proof sketch: write g = e^{2u} g_0. Both curvatures equal −1, so Δu = e^{2u} − 1 in suitable sign conventions. The maximum principle at the extrema of u then gives u ≡ 0. Alternatively, lift to H and use Schwarz–Pick.

(2) Case: compact of genus 1, connected (or not). In the oriented case X is a complex elliptic curve. Its universal cover is the complex affine line C. That line carries a Euclidean (flat Hermitian) metric, canonical up to a scalar factor. The metric is invariant under translations, and under all automorphisms of C, i.e. affine maps z ↦ az + b, it is invariant up to scalars. Hence it descends to X. The page breaks off at 'La constante multiplicative est …'. Presumably Grothendieck then fixes the constant by a normalization such as total area 1, since curvature 0 does not fix the scale.

The purpose is a systematic choice of a canonical metric for each conformal surface: hyperbolic (curvature −1), flat up to scale (genus 1 and the other parabolic cases), and spherical. This metric is the input for the 'surgery' (gluing) of conformal surfaces that the dossier pursues.
errors: No mathematical error. Two small imprecisions only. First, the flat metric on C is invariant under all affine maps only up to the scalar |a|^2. Second, uniqueness up to scalar on a compact genus-1 surface needs the observation that a flat metric conformal to the given one differs from it by e^{2u} with u harmonic, hence constant. Both points are implicit.

ideas.what: On a compact hyperbolic Riemann surface, the Poincaré metric is the unique conformal metric of constant curvature −1.
ideas.modern_name: Uniformization / Poincaré metric; uniqueness of the constant-curvature metric in a conformal class
ideas.usually_credited_to: Poincaré, Koebe (uniformization); uniqueness via the maximum principle (classical, e.g. Picard, Berger)

ideas.what: A genus-1 surface carries a flat metric, canonical up to scalar, descending from the translation-invariant metric on C. This extends to non-orientable quotients (the Klein bottle) via the orientation double cover.
ideas.modern_name: Flat metric on an elliptic curve / flat tori and Klein bottles

ideas.what: A systematic canonical-metric normalization for possibly non-orientable conformal surfaces, sorted by universal-cover type, as groundwork for 'surgery' of conformal surfaces.
ideas.modern_name: Canonical metrics on Klein surfaces / dianalytic surfaces

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard textbook account of the uniformization metrics (hyperbolic and flat cases). The only mildly distinctive features are the inclusion of non-orientable surfaces and the use of the material as preparation for a surgery program. Nothing new appears on this page.
transcription_corrections: '(ou un[?] tore[?])' should probably read 'affine', i.e. 'une droite complexe affine'.
'celle-ci aura métrique' is likely 'celle-ci a une métrique'.
'(métrique hermitienne)' could also be 'euclidienne'; the handwriting is ambiguous, and either reading is mathematically apt.
'(et qui sont par[?] tout automorphisme' is likely '(et même par tout automorphisme', invariant up to scalars.
'qui passe[?] des courbes[?] à X' is likely 'qui passe donc au quotient X'.
The page ends mid-sentence: 'La constante multiplicative est'.
